{#g9eu} # Discussion

{#tkeq} This prospective, multicenter phase II study evaluated the efficacy and safety of ICI combined with Hybrid-RT in patients with metastatic driver gene-negative NSCLC. Hybrid-RT is selected based on individual lesions. It adopts a dose-fractionation regimen characterized by short-course, low-total-dose radiotherapy. This approach theoretically reduces toxicity to organs at risk and minimizes radiation-induced immunosuppression, making it more suitable for combination with ICI therapy [@w:w20]. The study met its primary endpoint, with a 1-year PFS rate of 54.2% and a median PFS of 16.1 months, representing clinically meaningful and highly promising outcomes.

{#x7j4} In this trial, radiotherapy was administered during ICI maintenance after chemoimmunotherapy. Platinum-based chemoimmunotherapy achieves maximal tumor response in the induction phase but carries substantial toxicity. Thus, most novel ICI combinations are increasingly investigated in the maintenance setting [@w:w21]. Our sequential design was rationally constructed to avoid additive toxicity from concurrent chemo-immunoradiotherapy and minimize target volumes by delivering focal radiotherapy in the setting of reduced tumor burden. This optimized treatment sequence appears to account for both the promising survival efficacy and the favorable safety outcomes.

{#c6od} # Background

{#gqm7} Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) comprises heterogeneous pathological subtypes and molecular profiles . From a molecular and therapeutic perspective, NSCLC can be broadly categorized into 2 groups: driver gene-positive and driver gene-negative. While immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have provided substantial clinical benefit to patients with driver gene-negative tumors, a substantial proportion of those with advanced disease still do not achieve long-term survival [@w:w1]. Therefore, overcoming immune resistance remains a major therapeutic challenge.

{#rjqg} Radiotherapy plays a role in the treatment of NSCLC at almost all stages. Accumulating clinical evidence has demonstrated synergism between radiotherapy and immunotherapy [@w:w2], whereby radiotherapy enhances the efficacy of ICIs in both early- and advanced-stage NSCLC [@w:w3]. Preclinical studies indicate that radiotherapy promotes antitumor immunity by inducing immunogenic cell death (ICD) and remodeling the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). The core mechanism by which radiotherapy exerts antitumor effects involves ionizing radiation-induced DNA damage, which activates ICD pathways. This can convert irradiated tumor cells into an in situ tumor vaccine, triggering systemic antitumor responses in nonirradiated distant lesions, a phenomenon known as the abscopal effect [@w:w4].
